CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reversing only the denominator endpoints in a secant slope.
Interpreting a negative output as a decreasing function.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The sign of f(x) and the direction of change are different properties.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a local maximum as an absolute maximum on ℝ.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A graph can rise higher outside the local neighborhood.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State domain and compare all outputs before claiming absolute.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Connecting increasing intervals across an excluded input.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An asymptote separates the permitted domain into distinct pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Report separate intervals around a missing input.

ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goals: calculate average rates from tables, formulas and plotted endpoints, interpret change signs and physical units, identify increasing/decreasing/constant intervals, estimate local extrema and distinguish them from absolute extrema.
Secant slope between a<b is Δy/Δx=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a). Use the same input order for both differences; use output-units per input-units.
A positive rate describes increasing net output over an interval; a negative rate describes decreasing net output. A local slope may vary inside the interval.
Increasing/decreasing intervals describe behavior reading the graph from left to right, not whether y is positive or negative. Report open input intervals around turning points when appropriate.
Local extrema depend on a neighborhood; absolute extrema compare all permitted inputs. Always state the graph's domain, including any open endpoints and asymptotes.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down — (a) Compute average change of h(t)=t²+2t from t=1 to t=4. (b) Classify increasing/decreasing intervals for f(x)=x² on ℝ. (c) Explain why an increasing graph may have a negative output.
Independent Try It 1 — Compute a rate from recorded prices. A fare rises from $2.20 in 2019 to $2.80 in 2023. Find the average change per year.
Independent Try It 2 — Average rate with a radical. For f(x)=x−2√x, compute average rate on [1,9].
Independent Try It 3 — Symbolic average rate. For f(x)=x²+2x−8 find average rate on [5,a] with a≠5.
Independent Try It 4 — Use local extrema to classify monotonicity. Graph f(x)=x³−6x²−15x+20. Approximate the two local extrema and increasing/decreasing intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Average rate of change
KeyConcepts.Definition: The secant slope between inputs a and b is (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the SAME ordered endpoints in numerator and denominator.
KeyConcepts.Example: f(2)=7 and f(5)=1 implies average rate −2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rate units and sign
KeyConcepts.Definition: A change in output per one input unit has output-units/input-units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Negative average rate means outputs fall as inputs increase across the interval.
KeyConcepts.Example: Dollars per year and miles per hour are different units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Increasing, decreasing and constant
KeyConcepts.Definition: Increasing means outputs rise as x moves right; decreasing means outputs fall; constant means no change.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Monotonic intervals are input intervals, not output ranges.
KeyConcepts.Example: y=x² is decreasing for x<0 and increasing for x>0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Local extrema
KeyConcepts.Definition: A local maximum/minimum is the highest/lowest value among nearby inputs in the domain.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Local extrema do not necessarily dominate all values in the full domain.
KeyConcepts.Example: x³−3x has local maximum 2 at x=−1 and local minimum −2 at x=1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Absolute extrema
KeyConcepts.Definition: The absolute maximum/minimum is greatest/least output over the ENTIRE given domain.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A bounded domain can attain its extremum at a boundary; an unbounded curve might not attain an absolute maximum.
KeyConcepts.Example: The bounded graph with outputs −10..16 attains both absolute extremes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain-aware graphical reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: A continuous graph may have turning points, jumps, asymptotes and clipped viewing windows.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not infer global extrema from a clipped plot, and do not join intervals across excluded x.
KeyConcepts.Example: For 3/x+x/2, never combine monotonicity across x=0.

SummaryPoints: Average rate of change equals output change divided by input change; units are output units per input unit.
Use the same two endpoints in the numerator and denominator of the secant slope.
Increasing/decreasing/constant intervals depend on the graph's direction, not the sign of the output.
Local extrema describe a neighborhood; absolute extrema compare every permitted output.
Use domain restrictions and included endpoints when reasoning about global extrema.
First-party graph sketches and open-ended extrema are teacher-reviewed in Stage C.

WorkedExamples.Title: Average change in a time series
WorkedExamples.Question: An independently collected annual cost series rises from $2.50 per unit in 2020 to $3.10 per unit in 2024. Find average change per year.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: The year input changes by four years.
WorkedExamples.Check: The rate is positive because the dependent cost increased.

WorkedExamples.Title: Average slope from two plotted points
WorkedExamples.Question: A plotted continuous function passes through (−1,4) and (2,1). Compute average rate on [−1,2].
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Reversing exactly one subtraction changes the sign incorrectly.

WorkedExamples.Title: Average speed from measured distance
WorkedExamples.Question: A vehicle's distance from the starting position changes from 6 miles at t=0 hours to 276 miles at t=6 hours. Find average speed.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Average speed over the whole interval is not necessarily the instantaneous speed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Average change from a formula
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=x²−2/x, find the average rate over [2,4].
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both endpoints lie in the domain (x≠0).

WorkedExamples.Title: Average inverse-square force change
WorkedExamples.Question: A hypothetical force obeys F(d)=6/d² newtons for distance d>0 cm. Find the average force change over [2,6].
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Sign negative reflects force decreasing with distance.

WorkedExamples.Title: Symbolic endpoint rate
WorkedExamples.Question: For g(t)=t²+4t+2, compute the average change from t=0 to t=a, a≠0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: Factor a and cancel only because a≠0.

WorkedExamples.Title: Monotonic intervals from a graph
WorkedExamples.Question: A continuous graph rises over (1,3), falls over (3,4) and rises again for t>4. Identify all increasing intervals.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: Read graph direction left to right.
Increasing where output rises, not where the graph lies above x-axis.
Exclude turning-point boundaries under conventional open interval reporting.
WorkedExamples.Check: A graph can decrease while staying above zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Local extrema of a rational-plus-linear rule
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=3/x+x/2, x≠0, locate local extrema and intervals of increasing/decreasing.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: Stationary inputs satisfy x²=6, giving x=±√6.
The derivative is positive where |x|>√6 and negative where 0<|x|<√6.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Local maximum (−√6,−√6); local minimum (√6,√6). Increasing (−∞,−√6) and (√6,∞); decreasing (−√6,0) and (0,√6).
WorkedExamples.Check: Never cross the excluded input x=0 when writing monotonic intervals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Local extrema from an independently specified cubic
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=x³−3x, identify local extrema and their values.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: Derivative f'(x)=3x²−3 vanishes at x=−1 and x=1.
Sign changes from positive to negative at −1, and negative to positive at 1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Local maximum at (−1,2); local minimum at (1,−2).
WorkedExamples.Check: Local extrema need not be absolute extrema on the full real domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Absolute extrema on a complete displayed bounded model
WorkedExamples.Question: Connect successive independent graph points (−3,0),(−2,16),(−1,10),(0,0),(1,10),(2,16),(3,−10) with straight segments over [−3,3]. Find absolute max/min.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute, interpret and justify every mathematical conclusion with correct input and output units and graph limitations.
Steps: All seven points and connecting segments lie in the declared domain [−3,3].
The greatest displayed output is 16 at two inputs −2 and 2.
The least displayed output is −10 at the right included endpoint x=3.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Absolute maximum 16 attained at x=−2 and x=2; absolute minimum −10 at x=3.
WorkedExamples.Check: On a continuous piecewise-linear graph, extrema are at vertices or included endpoints.
